text: Show almost anyone two answers to the same question, and they can usually tell you which one is better, even if they could never have written the better one themselves. Judging is easier than demonstrating. Learning from human preferences turns that easy judgement into a training signal, and this lesson looks at the mechanism behind the two best known ways of doing it.

The raw data is a prompt, two responses, and a label saying which one a person preferred. To learn from it, we imagine that every response carries a hidden score, and that the chance a person prefers one response over the other is the sigmoid of the difference between their scores, the same squashing curve as in logistic regression. This is the Bradley-Terry model, proposed in the nineteen fifties for paired comparisons, such as tasters choosing between two samples. It only cares about differences, so adding the same constant to every score changes nothing.

In OpenAI's InstructGPT recipe, a reward model is trained on these comparisons. It is the language model with its output layer replaced by a single number, the score. Its loss is minus the log of the sigmoid of the preferred score minus the rejected score, so each comparison pushes the chosen answer up and the rejected one down, and the result is a stand-in for the human judge that can score any new response instantly.

Next, the language model is trained with reinforcement learning to write responses the reward model scores highly. Left alone, this goes wrong in a predictable way: the model finds quirks that the reward model overrates, much as a student can learn the examiner's habits instead of the subject. So the objective subtracts a penalty for drifting away from the starting model, measured by the log ratio of the two models' probabilities and scaled by a coefficient called beta, which keeps the text close to what the model could already write. InstructGPT optimised this with an algorithm called PPO, and its labellers preferred a model with one point three billion parameters over the original GPT-3, which is more than a hundred times larger.

The price is complexity. During this stage the training run juggles the model being trained, a frozen reference copy, the reward model and a value model, and it must generate fresh samples as it learns, which makes it slow and sensitive to its settings.

In twenty twenty-three, Rafailov and colleagues at Stanford pointed out that this objective has a known best answer. For any reward function, the policy that maximises reward minus the drift penalty is the reference model's distribution, reweighted by the exponential of the reward divided by beta, and then renormalised. Turn that equation around, and the reward can be written in terms of the policy itself: beta times the log of the ratio between the new model's probability and the reference model's, plus a term that depends only on the prompt.

Now substitute that expression into the Bradley-Terry loss. The prompt-only term is identical for both responses, so it cancels in the difference, and what remains is a simple classification loss on the language model itself, which raises the log ratio of the preferred answer relative to the rejected one. There is no separate reward model and no sampling during training, which is why their paper is subtitled, your language model is secretly a reward model.

Both methods are only as good as the preferences behind them, and both rely on the leash to the reference model to stay sensible. Many variants have followed, and which works best in practice is still an open question. Next, we turn from training to generation, and to the memory a model needs as its text grows longer: context windows and the KV cache.
